newsitem.title: CANADA: More carriers lift Atlantic cargo fuel surcharges.
newsitem.headline: More carriers lift Atlantic cargo fuel surcharges.

text.p: Market forces have tolled the virtual end to air cargo fuel surcharges on the North Atlantic and to Latin America, with the announcement Tuesday by three more North American airlines they are dropping the levy.
The transpacific market is another story. There, a majority of carriers are hanging on to fuel surcharges, reflecting a number of factors, including robust market conditions.
April has ushered in the traditional spring trough for North Atlantic cargo markets, say the carriers.

American Airlines, Northwest Airlines and Canadian Airlines International followed the lead of competitors by announcing plans Tuesday to scrap their North Atlantic surcharges, typically 10 cents a kg.
American cited the need to remain competitive with other carriers dropping the surcharge.
Of the three, only CAI also dropped the surcharge on Pacific routes.

"Fuel is a larger component of the costs on the Pacific," said Northwest spokesman Doug Killian. Northwest is a major freighter operator on the Pacific. Also fuel purchased in a number of Asian markets remain higher than elsewhere, he said.
American's decision takes effect April 28, at which time it will also drop a surcharge on southbound traffic to Latin America, said Mark Najarian, vice-president of sales for AA Cargo.
Northwest is dropping its domestic and North Atlantic surcharges immediately, while Canadian is dropping its international surcharge immediately, and its domestic surcharge on June 1.

The trend to drop surcharges was started in late March by Atlanta-based Delta Airlines. It got a major boost when United Airlines, a major Pacific player, dropped its surcharge on April 7. Most major European carriers are dropping theirs this week.
Notable holdouts on the North Atlantic are British Airways and Continental Airlines.
Continental Cargo marketing manager Dana Bates told Reuters on Tuesday her airline's fuel costs have not come down sufficiently and it will retain the surcharge indefinitely.
That's a lament of most airlines - while fuel prices are off their peak of last fall when they spiked to their highest since the 1991 Gulf War, they remain above year-ago levels in many markets.
Several carriers, including American and Canadian, have announced rate increases which take effect in the May and June time frame.
Many analysts see further downward pressure on fuel prices.
The spot price for benchmark West Texas Intermediate crude is down over $6 a barrel from its $26 winter peak.
Many analysts are forecasting a further dip to around $18/barrel by mid-year.
Fuel prices reflect a number of factors, such as the price of crude feedstocks, but also the amount of refinery capacity allocated to jet kerosene production.

This week's U.S. inventory report from the American Petroleum Institute, released late Tuesday, shows U.S. jet fuel stocks are 13 percent higher than at this time last year. -Air Cargo Newsroom Tel +44 171 542 7706 Fax +5017
